messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The burning aid station still dictates Sameer’s reality. He had been organizing evacuations when shelling collapsed the makeshift tent, sending him scrambling through choking fire and the deafening shouts of panicked, grieving crowds. When a plume of smoke drifts from a neighborhood barbecue or a colleague’s voice sharpens into anger, that sensory cue immediately pulls his torso back into the soot-stained position of that night, leaving him unable to sequence what happened first. These involuntary flashbacks confirm his crumbling conviction that the world operates on chaos and that he failed to protect the civilians trapped inside. Because he believes he is fundamentally broken and set apart, he instinctively turns away from funerals and graves, covering his face with his hands to block out the world. By deliberately avoiding positive events and retreating to isolated corners, he denies himself any corrective experience, keeping his traumatic recall trapped in a fragmented loop. This self-imposed distance only deepens his isolation and reinforces his belief that he should have done more. The narrowing of his daily routine makes him hyper-aware of any approaching anger or distant smoke. His shattered worldview has rewired his nervous system; the conviction that he failed and that safety is an illusion keeps him awake, scanning the dark long after his wife falls asleep. This relentless night vigilance makes him jump at ordinary household sounds, which in turn exhausts his capacity to focus, leaving the event’s timeline perpetually disjointed. The confusion of his recall deepens his conviction that he should have protected others, and this mounting shame makes him hyper-aware of any approaching anger or smoke. He knows that if he allows himself to feel hopeful, he will be punished, so he actively avoids moments of joy. The narrowing of his daily routine makes him more sensitive to ordinary sounds, which heightens his night vigilance. Now thirty-five, Sameer navigates the fluorescent silence of his tax consulting office, but his daily environment has become a minefield of avoided triggers. When the office coffee machine hisses or a client’s tone rises, he jumps, his concentration shattering as he instinctively covers his face with his hands. He avoids positive department gatherings, fearing that any moment of happiness will be stripped away, and this avoidance keeps his traumatic memories fragmented and his belief that he failed unchallenged. He finally sought help because the isolation has left his marriage emotionally barren, and he is most afraid that his avoidance will permanently erase his capacity for trust. He hopes to finally separate the present from the past, to stop hiding his face, and to believe that the world can be rebuilt.
